questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count steps in a simple route
questions.stem: From the numbers, converting benzene to bromobenzene then to phenylmagnesium bromide and finally to benzoic acid with carbon dioxide requires how many synthetic operations?
questions.explanation: The route involves bromination of benzene, formation of the Grignard reagent with magnesium, and carboxylation with carbon dioxide followed by workup, giving three distinct synthetic operations.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count atoms in the ethylene monomer
questions.stem: From the numbers, how many carbon atoms are present in the ethylene monomer used to make polyethylene?
questions.explanation: Ethylene is CH2=CH2 with two carbon atoms, and its polymerization gives a chain of repeating CH2-CH2 units.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count steps added by a protecting group
questions.stem: From the numbers, using a protecting group typically adds how many extra synthetic steps to a sequence?
questions.explanation: A protecting group strategy adds at least two steps, one to install the protecting group and one to remove it, which is why chemists avoid protection when a selective reagent is available.
questions.hint: One to install, one to remove.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count monomers in a nylon repeat
questions.stem: From the numbers, nylon-6,6 is made from a diamine and a diacid. How many different monomer types does it use?
questions.explanation: Nylon-6,6 is a condensation polymer made from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, two different monomers whose alternating condensation gives the polyamide chain.
questions.hint: Two monomers, a diamine and a diacid.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count carbon atoms added by carboxylation
questions.stem: From the numbers, reacting a Grignard reagent with carbon dioxide adds how many carbon atoms to the organic fragment?
questions.explanation: Carboxylation with carbon dioxide adds a single carbon atom, the carbon of carbon dioxide, to the carbon bearing magnesium, giving a carboxylate and after workup a carboxylic acid with one more carbon.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain disconnection logic
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is retrosynthetic analysis done from the target backward?

answer.exemplar: Working backward from the target lets the chemist choose disconnections that correspond to reliable, high-yielding reactions, reducing a complex molecule to simpler precursors step by step; this converges on commercially available starting materials more efficiently than trying random forward reactions from many possible starting points.

questions.explanation: Known reactions guide each disconnection. Working backward from the target lets the chemist choose disconnections that correspond to reliable, high-yielding reactions, reducing a complex molecule to simpler precursors step by step; this converges on commercially available starting materials more efficiently than trying random forward reactions from many possible starting points.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain ideal protecting group properties
questions.stem: Explain the following: what makes a good protecting group?

answer.exemplar: A good protecting group is easy to install selectively, stable to all the reagents used in the intervening steps, and easy to remove under mild conditions that do not disturb the rest of the molecule; it should also allow the chemist to control which functional group reacts at each stage.

questions.explanation: Install easily, survive the sequence, remove cleanly. questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain addition versus condensation
questions.stem: Explain the following: why do addition and condensation polymers have different atom economies?

answer.exemplar: Addition polymers form by opening unsaturated monomers so every atom of the monomer appears in the polymer with no byproduct, giving perfect atom economy, whereas condensation polymers eliminate a small molecule such as water at each linkage, so some atoms of the monomers are lost as byproduct rather than retained in the chain.

questions.explanation: Addition keeps all atoms; condensation loses small molecules.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain chemo-selectivity
questions.stem: Explain the following: why might a synthesis require a reagent that reacts with only one of two similar functional groups?

answer.exemplar: When a molecule has two similar reactive groups, an unselective reagent would modify both and give mixtures or overreaction; a selective reagent or a protecting group strategy allows one group to be transformed while the other is left intact, which is essential for building complex molecules with control.

questions.explanation: Selectivity avoids unwanted side reactions. When a molecule has two similar reactive groups, an unselective reagent would modify both and give mixtures or overreaction; a selective reagent or a protecting group strategy allows one group to be transformed while the other is left intact, which is essential for building complex molecules with control.
questions.hint: Control over which group reacts is essential.

questions.stem: Provide the explanation: why do addition and condensation polymers have different atom economies?

answer.exemplar: Addition polymers form by opening unsaturated monomers so every atom of the monomer appears in the polymer with no byproduct, giving perfect atom economy, whereas condensation polymers eliminate a small molecule such as water at each linkage, so some atoms of the monomers are lost as byproduct rather than retained in the chain.

questions.explanation: Addition keeps all atoms; condensation loses small molecules.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain chemo-selectivity
questions.stem: Provide the explanation: why might a synthesis require a reagent that reacts with only one of two similar functional groups?

answer.exemplar: When a molecule has two similar reactive groups, an unselective reagent would modify both and give mixtures or overreaction; a selective reagent or a protecting group strategy allows one group to be transformed while the other is left intact, which is essential for building complex molecules with control.

questions.explanation: Selectivity avoids unwanted side reactions. When a molecule has two similar reactive groups, an unselective reagent would modify both and give mixtures or overreaction; a selective reagent or a protecting group strategy allows one group to be transformed while the other is left intact, which is essential for building complex molecules with control.
questions.hint: Control over which group reacts is essential.
